clinicalPearls: A congenital or early-onset, well-defined, off-white hypopigmented (not fully depigmented) patch that is stable in relative size and does not progress
Often has a serrated or block-like/segmental configuration and remains fixed in its distribution
Distinguished from vitiligo, which shows chalky-white complete depigmentation and tends to spread, and in which Wood-lamp accentuation is far more stark
Differentiated from naevus anaemicus, a vascular anomaly that vanishes with diascopy and lacks true pigment loss
Reflects a functional melanocyte defect with normal or slightly reduced melanocyte numbers but impaired melanosome transfer
It is benign; management is reassurance, with cosmetic camouflage and photoprotection of the pale area if desired
The patch grows in proportion to the child rather than extending independently
reference.pathophysiology: Naevus depigmentosus is a mosaic developmental defect in which melanocytes are present in normal or slightly reduced numbers but function abnormally, with defective melanosome formation and impaired transfer of melanosomes to keratinocytes. Melanin is therefore reduced rather than absent, producing hypopigmentation rather than the complete depigmentation of vitiligo. Because it is a fixed developmental anomaly, the lesion remains stable throughout life.
additionalInvestigations: Wood-lamp examination showing off-white rather than chalky-white change
Examination for other features of tuberous sclerosis or mosaic disorders
Skin biopsy only rarely, when the diagnosis is uncertain
redFlags: Multiple ash-leaf macules or other features suggesting tuberous sclerosis
Segmental depigmentation that is spreading, raising the possibility of vitiligo
An extensive whorled or streaky pattern with systemic features suggesting hypomelanosis of Ito
reference.prognosis: The lesion is benign, stable and permanent, enlarging only in proportion to body growth, and carries no health risk beyond its cosmetic effect.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as vitiligo, or vice versa
Overlooking tuberous sclerosis when hypopigmented macules are multiple
Confusing it with naevus anaemicus by omitting diascopy
Attempting active repigmentation of a stable developmental lesion
management: Reassure that the lesion is a benign, stable developmental anomaly that needs no active medical treatment
Offer cosmetic camouflage for the hypopigmented patch where it is cosmetically troublesome
Advise photoprotection with sunscreen of the pale area, which lacks protective melanin and burns readily
Confirm the diagnosis clinically, distinguishing it from vitiligo and naevus anaemicus, reserving biopsy for uncertain cases
Examine for features of tuberous sclerosis or other mosaic disorders where the presentation is atypical
Monitor for stability, expecting the lesion to enlarge only in proportion to body growth
